# Component catalog (auto-generated)

> Regenerate with `manage.py sync_component_catalog` after any change under
> `content-pipeline/components/`. This is the authoritative "every component + what
> it is FOR" list the article author reads ON DEMAND (the brief keeps only the
> reader's-JOB mapping table). Pick by `when_to_pick`, never by a similar-sounding
> id; then open that component's `manifest.json` for its `schema`.

<!-- AUTOGEN:component-catalog START — regenerate with: manage.py sync_component_catalog -->
     **charts**
     - `chart_area` — Show how a metric moves across an ordered axis (time, or any continuous progression) — an equity curve, cumulative P&L, account balance, drawdown vs recovery, slippage vs spread. Pass a single `values` series for one filled area, OR pass `datasets` (1-4 series) to overlay/compare lines on the same axis. This is THE trend-over-an-ordered-axis chart (it absorbed the old standalone line chart). Reach for chart_bar when the x-axis is discrete categories rather than an ordered progression; for the underwater equity view use drawdown_chart; for a single bounded score use gauge_meter.
     - `chart_bar` — Compare one numeric metric across 2-8 discrete categories, ideally with two series side-by-side per category so the gap between them is the story (e.g., backtest vs. live win rate per strategy, p50 vs. p99 latency per broker type, or expected vs. realized return per asset). Reach for chart_area instead when the x-axis is time or a continuous progression; use chart_stacked_bar when the series sum to a whole.
     - `chart_doughnut` — Show how one whole splits into parts when the relative SHARE of each part is the story, not its exact value — capital allocation across instruments, where a monthly trading budget goes, win/loss/break-even mix, or risk spread across strategies. The card frames a crisp HTML title, a center total in the hole, and a legible value+share legend so the reader gets the composition at a glance. Cap at 6 slices; reach for chart_bar when you need to compare two series, or chart_stacked_bar when parts also accumulate across a time axis.
     - `chart_stacked_bar` — Show how a running total breaks down into stacked components across a time axis or discrete categories — monthly net P&L decomposed into gross pips vs commissions vs slippage, equity contribution by strategy, or cost composition over time. Best when BOTH the cumulative total and the share of each part carry the point; the optional summary strip lets you headline the net result the stack proves.
     - `correlation_matrix` — Show the pairwise correlations between 3-10 instruments (FX pairs, crypto, indices, metals) as a heatmap. Use it to expose hidden over-exposure — e.g. long EUR/USD + long GBP/USD at +0.86 is really one EUR-weighted bet, not diversification. Cells use a theme-aware diverging scale: green for positive (aligned) correlation, red for negative (inverse), faint neutral near zero, with an axis legend. Pass a square matrix whose rows/cols match the symbols order; the diagonal is always 1.
     - `cost_breakdown_bar` — Show how the all-in cost of a single trade splits across its components — spread, commission, swap/financing and optional slippage — as one horizontal stacked bar where each segment's width is proportional to its share of the total. A colour-coded legend lists every segment with its value and percentage, and the all-in TOTAL is shown prominently. Pure HTML/CSS (no JS, renders instantly). Pick it when explaining the true cost of trading, comparing raw-spread+commission vs all-in-spread accounts, breaking down round-turn cost, illustrating overnight financing/carry, or showing why a tight headline spread is not the whole picture.
     - `gauge_meter` — Show a single bounded number as a position on a colored semicircular arc — a speedometer-style gauge with low/medium/high (or sell/neutral/buy) zone bands, a needle pointing at the current value, and a large value readout with its zone label. Pick it whenever an article reduces a state to one score on a scale: market-sentiment / fear-and-greed indices (0–100), RSI or other bounded oscillators, a volatility or risk level, account-health or margin-usage percentage, prop-firm drawdown headroom, or a backtest confidence/quality score. Use it when the *one number and which band it falls in* is the takeaway; use a chart instead when the trend over time matters.
     - `kpi_sparkline_card` — Hand the reader 1-6 headline performance numbers at a glance — win rate, profit factor, max drawdown, average R, Sharpe. Each card shows a big value with an optional signed delta arrow and an optional short hint. Add a `spark` series to a card to draw an inline trend sparkline where the recent direction matters as much as the number. This is THE headline-numbers component (it absorbed the old key-stats grid): use point values alone for a clean stat scorecard, or add sparklines when you have a short series per metric. For a single bounded 0-100 score use gauge_meter; for many rows of attributes use comparison_table.

     **compare**
     - `before_after` — Show two states side-by-side — strategy before/after an optimization, broker A vs broker B execution quality, bad vs good risk management. Each side can contain inline HTML (lists, mini-tables, callouts).
     - `chart_radar` — Compare 2-4 candidates across 4-8 dimensions on the same 0-100 scale — bot scoring across latency / cost / customizability / win rate / drawdown / ease-of-use. Best when each axis is normalized to the same unit.
     - `comparison_table` — Compare 2-6 items across 2-8 dimensions so the reader can scan side-by-side. Use the `green_red` variant when there are exactly two columns representing 'good' vs 'bad'. Cells support an optional tone ('success' / 'danger' / 'warning') for inline emphasis.
     - `scenario_cards` — Lay out a forecast or outlook as 2-4 side-by-side scenarios — classically bearish / base / bullish — each with a price target or outcome, an optional probability, and the drivers that would make it play out. Pick this for any market-forecast, price-projection or 'what could happen next' section where the point is the RANGE of outcomes and what tips the balance, not a single number. Tone each card by direction (bullish=up/green, bearish=down/red, neutral=base). For a head-to-head of two named options use versus_card; for many rows of attributes use comparison_table.
     - `versus_card` — Frame a binary choice the reader is weighing as a direct face-off — two named options, A vs B, with a central VS badge, 2-5 short points per side, and a one-line verdict each. Use it when the post pits two concrete things against each other (manual signals vs automated bot, market order vs limit order, scalping vs swing, ECN vs market-maker broker) and you want the contrast to read instantly. Set winner to crown a recommended side. For more than ~5 attributes per side, or when you need cell-by-cell attribute alignment, prefer comparison_table; for two states of one thing (before vs after) use before_after.

     **flows**
     - `decision_tree` — Show a branching trading decision as a fully-rendered top-down tree the reader can take in at a glance: a root decision, labelled branches (e.g. Yes / No, conditions met / not met), and terminal verdict cards toned success (take the trade / favourable path) or danger (skip it / risk path). Use to turn an 'it depends' rule into a visible flowchart of every path and outcome. This is a static HTML/CSS tree (no Mermaid), so it renders identically in print, RSS, and dark/light themes.
     - `how_it_works_steps` — Explain a short ordered process (3-6 steps) as connected numbered cards — e.g. how a TradingView webhook reaches a broker, how a deposit clears, or how a bot opens a trade. Pick this when each step is a discrete action with a one-line description and the sequence (1 -> 2 -> 3) is the point. For a time-axis (clock/quarters) use the timeline components instead; for branching logic use decision-tree.
     - `mermaid_flowchart` — Visualize a decision tree or branching process with 4-15 nodes. Best for 'how do you decide X' content where the reader benefits from following arrows. Use classDef accept/reject/warn (defined as 8-digit hex fills, never rgba) to highlight terminal nodes.
     - `mermaid_sequence` — Show a time-ordered message exchange between 2-5 actors when the reader needs to understand WHO talks to WHOM, in what order, and what comes back. Ideal for execution flows (TradingView webhook -> bot -> broker API -> matching engine -> fill), API request/response chains, order lifecycles, and handshake/auth sequences. Use alt/else blocks to contrast a success path against a reject/error path. Prefer a flowchart when the logic is branching decisions rather than messages over time.
     - `mermaid_state` — Visualize a state machine — a finite set of named states with explicit transitions. Ideal for an automated bot's operational lifecycle (idle → scanning → in-trade → closing → cooldown, plus a halted error state), an order's lifecycle (pending → working → filled/cancelled → reconciled), or a prop-firm challenge progression (phase 1 → phase 2 → funded → breach). Pick this over a flowchart when the subject is 'what mode is it in right now and how does it move between modes', not 'how do I decide'. Use classDef with 8-digit-hex fills to color states by meaning (active/green, risk/red, waiting/blue).
     - `timeline` — Walk the reader through a sequenced process with phases. Set orientation='vertical' (default) for a stacked list that holds longer bodies and a marker per step — best for rollouts, multi-week plans, or step-by-step procedures; the last step can be toned 'danger'/'warning' to call out kill-criteria / stop conditions. Set orientation='horizontal' for a compact left-to-right band of 3-6 short phases that read as a flow (e.g. a trading day: premarket -> London open -> NY close); keep titles and bodies short in this mode. For discrete numbered actions (do this, then that) use how_it_works_steps; for branching logic use decision-tree.

     **interactive**
     - `accordion_faq` — Surface 3-10 question-answer pairs at the end of an article. Each row is collapsed by default; click to expand. Search engines pick this up as FAQPage schema when wrapped in JSON-LD (article-level concern, not component-level).
     - `calculator` — ANY time the reader should plug in their own numbers and watch a result update live — position size, pip value, payout, break-even, expectancy, compounding, risk-of-ruin, spread cost, drawdown, leverage, anything. This is the ONE calculator component: you declare the inputs (number / slider / stepper / segmented / toggle), the output formulas (plain arithmetic over the input keys, with min/max/abs/round/clamp/sqrt/pow available), and how each result is formatted. The component builds the calculator for THAT specific need. Do not look for a pre-made calculator per topic — there is exactly one, and you shape it.
     - `checklist` — A before-deploy or pre-trade checklist the reader actually ticks off. Each tick draws a check mark and advances a progress fill bar; ticking the last item unlocks a 'complete' state, so readers feel rewarded for finishing. Use as a closer for actionable how-to articles. Keep items short, imperative, and verifiable (something the reader can confirm 'yes/no'). For a single misconception-trap question with one right answer use quiz_single instead.
     - `live_simulator_candlestick` — The marquee interactive widget for long-form articles: a bot opens and closes trades against a random-walk candlestick series while live stats (trade count, win rate, avg win/loss, net P&L) update tick by tick. It renders a full ghost-preview of the upcoming series at rest, so it looks alive before Play is pressed. Best for explaining strategy expectancy, why win rate varies run-to-run, or how TP/SL/hold rules behave. Pure SVG + JS, no external libraries. Pick this to WATCH trades open and close in real time; for the outcome spread across many runs use monte_carlo_simulator; for the EV map across the win-rate x R:R plane use expectancy_grid.
     - `quiz_single` — Insert a one-question check at the end of a tricky section to confirm the reader actually internalized the concept. Best for misconception traps where the intuitive answer is wrong. After the reader picks, it marks the correct option green and their wrong pick red, shows a pass/fail result line, and reveals a 'Why' explanation. Use when there is exactly one right answer and the wrong answers represent real, tempting mistakes.

     **reference**
     - `code_block` — Show actual code the reader can copy and run — MQL4/5 expert-advisor snippets, TradingView Pine Script, Python ccxt order placement, a webhook payload, a CLI command. Use for a focused excerpt (a function, a loop, a config), not a whole file; long programs belong in a gist. The polished header carries a language chip + optional filename; readers get a one-click copy button, and optional line numbers help you reference specific lines in the surrounding prose.
     - `formula_block` — Display a single key formula — Kelly fraction, expected value, Sharpe ratio, position size, R-multiple, pip value — as a standout reference block. Use when one equation is the centerpiece and deserves large monospace typography, an accent rail, and a 'where' note defining its variables. For a runnable code snippet use code_block instead; for multiple stacked equations use one formula_block per equation.
     - `risk_warning_callout` — Drop in the mandated compliance risk disclosure on any post or glossary term that discusses signals, backtests, win rates, leverage, or live trading outcomes. Use it once near the relevant claim (not decoratively); it carries a warning-styled box and a required link to the host's risk-warning page. Prefer this over a hand-written warning callout whenever the copy is a regulatory risk disclosure.

     **risk-performance**
     - `backtest_metrics_panel` — Show a full backtest report card: every metric a trader looks at (Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar, max DD, recovery factor, etc.) with a per-metric verdict color (good/bad/warn). Use when teaching what to look for in a backtest, or when reviewing a specific strategy.
     - `drawdown_chart` — Show the underwater equity curve — how deep and how long each drawdown lasted. Use after the article has discussed the difference between average return and worst-case drawdown. Always renders below zero with red fill.
     - `expectancy_grid` — Show where a strategy crosses from negative to positive EXPECTANCY across the win-rate × reward-to-risk (R:R) plane — a coloured grid where each cell is the expected value per $100 risked. Use it to prove that a high win rate alone is not enough: a 60% win rate at 0.5:1 R:R still loses money over time. The reader hovers any cell to read its exact EV. Theme-aware fills via window.cpTheme. Pick this when the takeaway is 'which win-rate × R:R combinations are actually profitable'; for a single trade's R:R ladder use risk_reward_visualizer. For the spread of outcomes from ONE edge over many simulated runs use monte_carlo_simulator; to watch trades open and close tick by tick use live_simulator_candlestick.
     - `monte_carlo_simulator` — Show how widely a single edge (win rate + reward-to-risk) spreads real outcomes. Renders an equity-curve fan of N (default 200) simulated runs with a 10th–90th-percentile band, a median path, and summary stats (median return, % profitable, worst drawdown, risk of ruin). A deterministic frame draws on load; Run re-rolls the seed, Reset returns to it. Use to set realistic expectations and to motivate position-sizing for the band, not the average. Pick this for the DISTRIBUTION of outcomes across many runs; for which win-rate x R:R combos are break-even use expectancy_grid; to watch a single run play out tick by tick use live_simulator_candlestick.
     - `risk_reward_visualizer` — Show a trade's entry, stop-loss and take-profit as a proportional price ladder: the risk zone (entry → SL, red) and reward zone (entry → TP, green) are shaded to scale so the reader sees the asymmetry at a glance, with a prominent reward-to-risk readout and the break-even win rate it implies. Direction (long/short) is detected automatically. Inputs are editable, so the visual updates live as the reader experiments with stop placement. Pick it when explaining position sizing, R-multiples, stop discipline, or why a higher R:R lets a lower win rate stay profitable.
     - `trade_log_table` — Show a realistic sample of a bot's trade log so readers see what win/loss distribution actually looks like — not just summary stats. Columns: date, symbol, side, entry, exit, pips, P&L. Highlights buy/sell tags and per-row P&L tone.

     **structure**
     - `beat_section` — Render a full article section whose chrome itself encodes the section's emotional beat — a colored left rail, a labeled beat tag with an icon, and a variant-specific callout — so a scanning reader instantly feels whether they are hearing about a problem, a complication, partial progress, the essential answer, or a call to act. Reach for this when a section's narrative role matters as much as its text and you want the surface to carry that role. Pick the variant by beat: 'problem_named' for an opening or stakes-naming section (red rail + a single hard stat callout); 'tension_rises' for a mid-article 'yes but' complication (amber rail + a bold pull-quote); 'partial_resolution' for one step of a multi-step methodology (accent rail + a step-progress bar and a 3-up workflow strip); 'full_payoff' for the section that delivers the article's essential answer (green frame + a result/metric answer card); 'next_action' for a closing or 'do this now' section (accent frame + numbered steps and a CTA). Use a plain callout component instead when the section carries no narrative-beat meaning.
     - `closing_loop` — The article's final block. Always loops back to the opening pain point and hands the reader one concrete next move, with the shape matched to the article's intent class. Pick variant='informational' when the reader's journey continues across pages (a loop line, a short synthesis paragraph, and 2-3 deeper-reading links). Pick variant='commercial' when the conclusion IS a recommendation (a loop line, one 'decide' card carrying logo+name+reason+CTA, plus an honest alt-path escape hatch for readers who can't take the pick). Pick variant='transactional' when the explicit goal is conversion (a centered loop line, a bold value reaffirmation, one big CTA, and a row of trust marks that mirror the transactional hero at the top of the article). Use exactly once, as the last visual in the piece.
     - `element_card` — Render a single content element with its role in the article made instantly legible. Pick variant 'essential' for the answer the searcher actually came for: an always-open, green-accented card with a role badge, the question it answers, a prominent answer heading, an optional label/value detail grid, and an optional source-attribution line — lift it into any section, an FAQ slot, or a TL;DR block. Pick variant 'complementary' for optional context that some readers want but most don't: a collapsible card with an 'Optional' role badge, a toggle title, body prose, and an optional supporting note; it stays collapsed by default (set open_by_default true to ship it expanded). Reach for this when you want one self-contained element whose importance is visually obvious, rather than a generic callout or a multi-row accordion (use accordion_faq for 3+ Q&A pairs).
     - `intent_hero` — Open an article with an above-the-fold hero matched to what the searcher actually came for, instead of a generic featured image. Choose the 'variant' from the post's search intent: 'informational' (answer-first) when the user wants one discrete fact NOW — current price, today's win rate, latency stat: it shows the question, a huge numeric answer with delta, a 4-cell context grid, an inline sparkline from a numbers array, and a source line. 'commercial' (top-pick + why) for 'best X' / 'X vs Y' / 'top N' comparison queries: a pain line, a crowned editor's-pick card with name, 1-5 reasons and an optional short QUALITATIVE verdict badge (what it's best FOR — never a fabricated numeric rating), up to 4 runner-up rows, and a meta/CTA footer. 'transactional' (CTA-first) for signup / free-trial / upgrade pages where the user has decided to act: eyebrow, headline (em-emphasis allowed), subline, a presentational email field + button (NO real submit), a reassurance line, and up to 4 trust items. 'navigational' (destination card) when the user searched for a known place ('the product admin panel'): breadcrumb, title, description, a primary CTA, and a row of related links. Use exactly once per article, at the very top. For mid-article calls-to-action use a callout; for plain headline stats use kpi_sparkline_card.

     **structure-maps**
     - `anatomy_diagram` — Teach the parts of a single visual subject by labeling them. A central inline-SVG subject (e.g. a candlestick, an order ticket, a chart pattern) sits in the middle and callout cards point to its parts with leader lines. Best for 'anatomy of X' / 'parts of a Y' explainers where the reader must connect each named part to its location on the picture. Pick the built-in 'candlestick' subject for OHLC explainers, or supply your own inline SVG via subject_svg for any other object.
     - `copy_trade_flow` — Show how a copy-trading (mirror-trading) relationship works: one leader/strategy account places a trade, and it is mirrored to each follower's account scaled to THEIR balance/risk — so the reader sees the proportional one-to-many mirroring, not just an org chart. The leader card shows the master trade; each follower card shows the position that trade becomes on that account. Pick it for copy-trading / mirror-trading / PAMM-style content explaining how copying allocates and scales. For a generic org/tier structure use hierarchy; for the step-by-step setup use how_it_works_steps.
     - `funnel` — Show how a population shrinks across the ordered stages of a journey — visitors -> sign-ups -> funded accounts -> active traders, signal-views -> broker clicks -> registrations -> deposits, or an IB recruitment funnel (leads -> calls -> sign-ups -> producing sub-IBs). Each stage is a proportional bar (width = its share of the top stage) with the count and the percent of the entry that survives to it, so the drop-off between steps is obvious. Pick this when the STORY is attrition through a sequence; for a non-shrinking ordered process use how_it_works_steps, and for parts of one whole use chart_doughnut.
     - `hierarchy` — Show a top-down structure of who sits above whom, or how tiers stack — most useful for the IB model (a Master IB above several sub-IBs above their traders), a partnership/commission hierarchy, account or membership tiers (Bronze -> Silver -> Gold), or a prop-firm progression of account sizes. An optional single apex node sits at the top; each level below is a row of one or more nodes, joined by branching connector lines. Pick this when the relationship is hierarchical (levels of an org/tier); for a sequence of actions use how_it_works_steps, for branching decisions use decision-tree, and for attrition through stages use funnel.
     - `ib_commission_tiers` — Show how an IB's (Introducing Broker's) earnings scale across volume or revenue-share tiers — the rate at each tier, what unlocks it, and an illustrative payout, with one tier flagged as the target/recommended tier. Pick it for IB & partnership content answering 'how much can I earn as an IB?', a rebate/commission rate card, or a Master-IB vs sub-IB split. For the IB org structure (who sits under whom) use hierarchy; for the IB recruitment drop-off use funnel; for an earnings what-if the reader computes live use calculator. Frame figures as illustrative examples, never promised income.

     **trade-visuals**
     - `annotated_price_chart` — Show a worked trade setup on a real-looking price chart: a price series (line or candlesticks) overlaid with annotation lines and zones — an entry level, a stop-loss line or zone (red/sell), a take-profit line or zone (green/buy), plus optional support/resistance levels and free-floating text callouts pinned to a candle. Pick it when you are walking the reader through a specific setup (a breakout long, a range fade, a pullback entry) and you want them to SEE where entry, risk and reward sit relative to structure — not just read numbers in a table. Static, dependency-free inline SVG: it renders the full chart on first paint with no chart library and no blank frame. Use the risk_reward_visualizer instead when you only need the proportional entry/SL/TP ladder without price action; use a Chart.js line/area chart when the point is the data trend itself rather than an annotated setup.
     - `binary_options_payoff` — Visualize the discontinuous payoff curve of a binary option — flat at -stake below the strike, flat at +payout above. Two-line SVG plot for Call and Put. Helps readers see why binary risk is bounded but win-rate must be high to be profitable.
     - `forex_session_clock` — A 24-hour UTC timeline of the four FX trading sessions (Sydney / Tokyo / London / New York) shown as colored bands on one track, with the high-liquidity OVERLAP windows highlighted (the Tokyo+Sydney and especially the London+New York overlap). A live vertical marker sweeps to the current UTC time and the open sessions are called out. The bands render server-side, so the timeline is fully readable even before JS runs. Use it to explain why intraday FX strategies cluster around the London/NY overlap, when liquidity and volatility peak, and which hours are dead.
     - `limit_tracker` — Track one or more current values against the limits they must respect, with a bar per rule showing how much headroom is left before a breach. Built for prop-firm / funded-account rules (daily-loss limit, max total drawdown, profit target, minimum trading days) but works for any value-vs-threshold read: margin usage, weekly risk budget used, exposure caps. Each row colours by how close it is. Set direction='max' (default) for a ceiling the value must stay UNDER (e.g. daily loss, drawdown), or 'min' for a floor/target it must reach (e.g. profit target, minimum trading days). Pick this when the takeaway is 'how close am I to breaking — or hitting — a rule'; for a single bounded score use gauge_meter.
     - `order_book_ladder` — Show a static snapshot of an order book (bid ladder + ask ladder + last price). Use when explaining liquidity, spread, market impact, or how a bot's order interacts with the book. Static data (mock) — no live feed.
